messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keilani was just six months into her first job as an auditor when the messages started. At first, they were from a forgotten name from a university class, friendly and innocuous. Then they became constant, referencing what she was wearing or who she was with. He started appearing outside her office building in downtown Honolulu, and then, terrifyingly, outside her apartment complex. For three months, her life was a map of his movements, a constant, low-grade hum of fear that spiked whenever she saw his car or heard her phone buzz. The restraining order finally made him stop, but the feeling of being watched never left.

In the year since, that feeling has calcified into a set of rigid, unshakeable beliefs. Keilani has come to believe that the world is a profoundly dangerous place, a conviction that has reshaped her existence. She is certain that the only way to remain safe is to be on guard at all times, a state of hypervigilance that leaves her perpetually exhausted. This constant sense of threat has bled into her perception of her own life; looking at her accounting degree on the wall, she feels a hollow ache. That ambitious young woman felt like a stranger, someone from a different, safer world. She was convinced her life had been destroyed by the trauma, its trajectory permanently and irrevocably altered for the worse.

These deeply held convictions govern her every action. Because she believes the world is dangerous, she has systematically dismantled her life outside her apartment. Going out is no longer a choice; it is a risk she cannot afford to take. Her groceries are delivered, she works remotely whenever possible, and the vibrant city she once loved now feels like a landscape of potential threats. Her apartment has become both a sanctuary and a prison, the only place the crushing weight of her hypervigilance eases even slightly. This retreat from the world is fueled by a darker, more insidious thought: a quiet but persistent belief that she deserves this suffering. She tells herself that if she had been smarter or less naive, she would have recognised the danger sooner. This shrunken life, she feels, is a penance she must pay for her failure to protect herself. The belief that her life has been destroyed makes any flicker of joy feel unearned and inappropriate. When her old friends invited her for a beach barbecue last month, the thought of laughter and sunlight felt almost offensive. Happiness, she felt, was for the person she used to be, and she now actively avoids any situation that might make her feel hopeful, as if embracing it would be a betrayal of the damage that was done.

Her work, once a source of pride, has become a source of acute stress. As an auditor, on-site client visits are a core part of her job. She has managed to postpone or delegate the last three, citing illness or technical issues, but her manager’s patience is wearing thin. The thought of entering an unfamiliar office building, of sitting in a lobby where anyone could walk past, is paralyzing. The professional life she worked so hard to build is now directly threatened by the very strategies she uses to feel safe. It was the email from her manager scheduling a formal performance review that finally pushed her to seek help. Keilani knows she cannot continue this way, but she is terrified that this is all she is now—a collection of fears and rigid rules. More than anything, she is afraid that her belief is true: that her life is already destroyed, and that therapy will only confirm it.
